# Results

## Reservoirs mark, but do not make, irrigated vulnerability

Across the matched design (21 dammed vs 244 control subcuencas), dammed basins contain
roughly an order of magnitude more cropland than matched controls — a mean of
11.1% of basin area versus 2.4% (@fig-area, panel a). This gap, however, is a
*siting* signature: it is present and stable across the entire 2000–2024 record, with
dammed and control trajectories evolving in parallel through the 2010-onset megadrought
(dashed line). A dynamic event study confirms this — the dammed × year coefficients on
cropland area are jointly flat before 2009 (Wald $p = 0.68$) and show no divergence after the
drought onset (@fig-area, panel b). Reservoirs mark where irrigated agriculture already
was; they do not detectably expand it or change how it responds to drought.

```{r}
#| label: fig-area
#| fig-cap: "Observed irrigated-area dynamics in dammed versus matched-control basins. (a) Weighted mean cropland area (% of basin, MapBiomas class 18); dammed basins hold ~10x more cropland but trajectories are parallel. (b) Dynamic event study (dammed x year, reference 2009): flat pre-trends and no post-megadrought divergence. Dashed line, 2010 megadrought onset."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_area_did.png")
```

## No operational reservoir effect survives once siting is matched out

We probe the operational vulnerability mechanism with four independent estimators (@tbl-main):
two cross-sectional doubly-robust matched ATTs — net irrigated-area expansion
($-0.69$ ha km^-2^, 95% CI $[-2.4, 1.1]$) and reservoir evapotranspiration buffering
($-0.014$ d log ET / d SPEI, $[-0.065, 0.037]$) — and forcing-interacted
difference-in-differences slope gaps on the observed area and ET panels, in which the
deficit dose is the meteorological SPEI rather than calendar time (so year fixed effects
absorb the common megadrought shock and the estimand is the differential deficit-to-impact
*slope*). Because the treatment is effectively time-invariant (18 of 24 reservoirs predate
the record), this within-unit, forcing-based design is the only defensible dynamic
identification; inference uses randomization of treatment within climate × aridity strata
(~21 treated clusters).

Every estimate straddles zero (@fig-forest). The forcing-interacted slope gap is null for
irrigated area ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.91$) and orchard ET ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.24$). The
whole-basin ET slope gap is nominally positive under cluster-robust errors but null under
randomization inference ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.11$), and its pre-trends fail
($p \approx 10^{-10}$) — a few-clusters over-rejection on a panel known to be confounded by
residual aridity over barren land; the ET conclusion therefore rests on the cross-sectional
buffering null. No panel exhibits the positive slope that the vulnerability mechanism
predicts, and none the negative slope that operational buffering would produce: conditional
on siting, the operational reservoir effect brackets zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Convergent null across estimators. Cross-sectional doubly-robust matched ATTs and forcing-interacted DiD slope gaps (treat:SPEI). DiD rows are judged by randomization-inference p-values (p); cluster-robust CIs are shown for completeness. A positive estimate would indicate induced-demand vulnerability; a negative one, operational buffering."
#| echo: false
tab <- data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_main_results.csv")
knitr::kable(tab[, .(Group = group, Outcome = outcome, Estimand = estimand,
                     Estimate = round(estimate, 3),
                     `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3g, %.3g]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                     p = ifelse(is.na(p), "-", sprintf("%.2f", p)), Verdict = verdict)])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| fig-cap: "Standardized dammed - control effect (estimate / SE) across all four estimators. DiD rows are standardized via their randomization-inference p-value. Dotted lines mark +/-1.96; every confidence interval spans zero."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_convergent_null.png")
```

## Bounding the null: what the design can rule out

A null is only informative against a stated effect size, so we convert each non-result into a
bound via equivalence testing (two one-sided tests) and a minimum detectable effect (MDE)
built from the permutation-null spread (@tbl-equiv). The streamflow design has the most power:
it can detect a buffering effect that attenuates SPEI→SSI transmission by ≳46% of the baseline
slope (MDE $0.27$ on a baseline of $0.59$; downstream-only $0.31$, ≳59%). No outcome's 90%
interval falls inside its pre-specified negligible region (±25% of baseline), so we do *not*
claim formal statistical equivalence to zero — with ~21 treated clusters the design can exclude
only **large** operational effects, not small ones. The causal weight of the null therefore
rests on the within-basin placebo below, not on equivalence: we can rule out the order of
buffering that would justify storage expansion as drought protection, and the placebo shows the
residual apparent effect is selection.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-equiv
#| tbl-cap: "Equivalence / minimum-detectable-effect bounds on the headline nulls. Observed slope gap, MDE (smallest effect detectable at 80% power from the permutation-null SD), the 90% (TOST) interval, and whether it lies within the negligible region (+/-25% of baseline). No outcome is formally equivalent to zero; the streamflow design rules out attenuations larger than ~46-59% of baseline transmission."
#| echo: false
eq <- data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_equivalence.csv")
knitr::kable(eq[, .(Outcome = outcome,
                    Observed = round(observed, 3),
                    MDE = round(mde, 3),
                    `90% CI` = sprintf("[%.3g, %.3g]", ci90_lo, ci90_hi),
                    `Equiv. to 0?` = ifelse(equivalent, "yes", "no"),
                    `p_perm` = round(p_perm, 2))])
```

## The apparent buffering is reservoir siting, not regulation

The preceding nulls use vegetation and ET proxies. We obtain the same answer on the direct,
vegetation-independent availability outcome — streamflow — and, uniquely here, can show *why* a
naive analysis would mislead. From CR2 daily gauge records (2000–2020) we build a 12-month
Standardized Streamflow Index (SSI-12) and test whether meteorological drought (SPEI-12)
propagates less strongly to streamflow drought in dammed than in matched-control basins
(@fig-streamflow). Dammed basins do show a flatter SPEI→SSI transmission — the visual signature
of buffering (@fig-streamflow, panel a). But this apparent attenuation **(i)** does not survive
randomization inference (intent-to-treat slope gap $-0.18$, cluster $p = 0.03$ but
$p_{\text{perm}} = 0.39$), and **(ii)** is present just as strongly at gauges located *upstream*
of the dam — which are physically unregulated — as at downstream gauges
($-0.20$ vs $-0.16$; @fig-streamflow, panel b). There is no downstream-versus-upstream
dose-response, the signature a genuine regulation effect would require. The flatter slope is
therefore a property of *where* reservoirs are sited — arid, hydrogeologically distinct basins —
not of the reservoirs themselves.

The siting interpretation is confirmed by the way the signal behaves across the aridity
gradient. The national "buffering" slope gap ($-0.16$ to $-0.20$) **collapses to ≈ $-0.03$ once
the comparison is made within climate region** — the textbook signature of a between-region
confound, in which arid treated basins are contrasted against a control pool spanning the whole
wet→dry gradient. In the high-supply south, where buffering should be easiest to detect, the
downstream and upstream gaps are statistically identical ($-0.036$ vs $-0.034$) and both
indistinguishable from zero (southern downstream $p_{\text{perm}} = 0.78$). Splitting by region
thus both kills the signal and equalizes the upstream and downstream reaches — two independent
confirmations that the attenuation is the aridity gradient, not regulation. Because the
upstream-of-dam comparison is unavailable for any vegetation outcome, streamflow provides the
cleanest within-design falsification: the effect a naive dammed-versus-control or calendar-time
analysis would report is siting, not regulation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-streamflow
#| fig-cap: "Streamflow buffering is reservoir siting, not regulation. (a) SPEI-12 to SSI-12 transmission for dammed versus matched-control basins (downstream gauges); dammed basins show a flatter slope, the apparent buffering. (b) Differential slope (treat:SPEI; <0 = buffering) for intent-to-treat, downstream-only, and the upstream-only placebo, with randomization-inference p-values. All are permutation-null, and the upstream placebo - above-dam, unregulated - is as strong as downstream, so the attenuation is siting/aridity, not the dam."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_streamflow.png")
```

## The binding constraint is inflow, not storage

If reservoirs neither buffer nor amplify drought operationally, what fails under the megadrought
is supply, not the structures — and the storage record bears this out (@fig-storage). Over
2005–2024 the entire storage band shifts downward in step: annual peak storage declines by
$-1.3$ percentage points of capacity per year ($p = 0.013$) and the annual trough falls almost
identically ($-1.2$ pp yr^-1^, $p < 10^{-4}$), while the seasonal amplitude is statistically
unchanged ($-0.06$ pp yr^-1^, $p = 0.91$). A band that drops without narrowing is the signature
of a supply-side level shift — less water arriving — not of a degraded buffer, which would
compress the amplitude. Reservoirs still convert meteorological surplus into storage as
efficiently as before; there is simply less and less to store. Under aridification the binding
constraint is therefore declining inflow, not storage capacity or operation, so expanding
storage is a supply-blind response to a supply problem [@li_diminishing_2023; @wang_reservoir_2024].

```{r}
#| label: fig-storage
#| fig-cap: "The binding constraint is inflow, not storage. (a) Cross-reservoir annual storage band - peak and trough percent-of-capacity (mean line, IQR ribbon) - drifts downward over 2005-2024 with roughly parallel trend lines: the whole band shifts while seasonal amplitude is unchanged. (b) Per-year trend slope of peak, trough, and amplitude (reservoir fixed effects, clustered SEs): peak and trough both decline while amplitude brackets zero - a supply-side level decline, not a refill/buffer degradation."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_storage_band.png")
```
